definition.text: The amount of a renewable resource people can harvest without over-harvesting or damaging it.

facts.text: Formally, it is the ecological yield that can be taken without shrinking the natural capital itself, keeping ecosystem services at the same level or higher.
It applies only to renewable resources, since extracting non-renewable resources always reduces natural capital.
It is often calculated as half the carrying capacity, the population level at which a stock can be harvested and still regrow.
It changes over time: a forest hit by a natural disaster needs more of its own yield to recover, so its sustainable yield falls.
It is used mostly in forestry, fisheries and groundwater, where a 'safe yield' marks the extraction rate beyond which an aquifer is overdrawn.
Overfishing in the mid-1850s led to maximum sustainable yield becoming a reference point for fishery management.
Sustainable yield forestry is criticised for focusing only on wood, changing landscapes and reducing biodiversity; the term has also been called anthropocentric.

definition.text: Economic use of oceans, lakes, rivers and coasts, generally with an emphasis on using their resources sustainably.

facts.text: There is no agreed definition; the World Bank calls it sustainable use of ocean resources for growth, livelihoods and jobs while preserving ocean ecosystem health.
It spans fisheries, aquaculture, shipping and tourism as well as emerging activities such as offshore renewable energy, blue carbon and seabed mining.
It also covers unpriced ocean ecosystem services such as carbon sequestration, coastal protection and biodiversity.
The term was popularised by the Rio+20 UN Conference on Sustainable Development in 2012.
Mangrove forests support more than 4 million fishers and protect coasts, yet 0.5% have been lost each year on average since the 2000s.
In 2023 the EU's blue economy employed nearly 4.9 million people and added €263 billion in gross value added.
Misleading claims about effects on aquatic environments have been called bluewashing, by analogy with greenwashing.

definition.text: Finance that cuts the carbon footprint of ocean-related activities and benefits the marine environment, as part of sustainable finance.

facts.text: The World Economic Forum estimates US$175 billion a year is needed to meet SDG 14, the most underfunded of the 17 goals.
It funds marine renewable energy, zero-emissions shipping and restoration of mangroves and seagrass meadows.

definition.text: A critical approach examining how blue economy and blue growth initiatives affect coastal communities and small-scale fisheries.

facts.text: It recognises small-scale fishing communities' historical rights to marine resources and coastal space, sometimes used for thousands of years.
It studies pressures on these fisheries from industrial fishing, tourism, aquaculture and energy production.

definition.text: Something drawn from nature and used with few changes, such as sunlight, air, water, land, minerals, plants and wildlife.

facts.text: Every man-made product is made, at bottom, from natural resources.
Some resources are renewable and are restored by natural processes, while many extractive industries rely on non-renewable resources that can be extracted only once.
Who gets natural resources is at the centre of many economic and political confrontations, especially when scarcity is increasing.
Resource extraction is a major source of human rights violations and environmental damage.
In 1982 the UN's World Charter for Nature recognised the need to protect nature from further depletion by human activity.
Natural resource management focuses on how managing land, water, soil, plants and animals affects quality of life for present and future generations.

definition.text: Ways of sorting natural resources by origin, stage of development, renewability and ownership.

facts.text: By origin, resources are biotic, from living things (including fossil fuels formed from decayed organic matter), or abiotic, from non-living material such as land, water and ores.
By stage of development, potential resources are known but unused, such as unextracted petroleum, while actual resources are surveyed and in use.
By ownership, resources can be individual, community, national or international, such as international waters.

definition.text: A war caused by conflict over resources, typically between whoever controls a resource and an aggressor who wants it.

facts.text: Industrialisation raised the raw materials nations need, and such power struggles have underlain conflicts since the late 19th century.
A classic example is the 19th-century conflict over guano, a nutrient-rich fertiliser, on Peru's Chincha Islands.
The geopolitical view sees resource conflict as strategic; the environmental security view sees it as a response to scarcity.
Conflicts can occur over control of resources and their revenues, one of the arguments linking resources with war.

definition.text: Natural resources extracted in a conflict zone and sold to keep the fighting going.

facts.text: The idea emerged in the late 1990s with 'blood diamonds' that financed rebellions in Angola and Sierra Leone, followed by 'conflict timber' in Cambodia and Liberia.
There is statistical and anecdotal evidence that precious commodities can prolong conflicts.
The US, EU and OECD treat tantalum, tin, tungsten and gold linked to conflict in the DRC as conflict minerals and require companies to report their use.
